blocks.text: The **Mughal Empire (1526–1857)**, founded by **Babur** at Panipat, was medieval India's grandest state. The **Great Mughals — Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb** — built and expanded it to near-subcontinental extent before its 18th-century decline.

rows: **1st Panipat (1526)** vs Ibrahim Lodi; **Khanwa (1527)** vs Rana Sanga; memoir **Baburnama** (Turki).
Lost to **Sher Shah Suri** (Chausa 1539, Kannauj 1540); regained throne 1555; **Sur interregnum** (Sher Shah's rupee, GT Road, dak).
**2nd Panipat (1556)** vs Hemu; mansabdari; **Din-i-Ilahi**; Rajput policy; abolished jizya.
Nur Jahan; captured Kangra; execution of Guru Arjan; Captain Hawkins/Sir Thomas Roe.
**Taj Mahal**; golden age of architecture; Deccan wars.
Greatest extent; re-imposed **jizya (1679)**; 27-yr Deccan/Maratha war; empire overstretched.

items: Battles: Panipat I (1526, Babur), Khanwa (1527), Panipat II (1556, Akbar vs Hemu).
Sher Shah Suri's interregnum (rupee, GT road, dak-chauki) is a frequent MCQ.

prelimsPointers: **First Battle of Panipat (1526)** — Babur defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** (used field artillery & tulughma).
**Battle of Khanwa (1527)** — Babur vs **Rana Sanga**; **Baburnama** written in **Turki**.
**Sher Shah Suri** — defeated Humayun; introduced the silver **rupiya**, rebuilt the **Grand Trunk Road**, **dak-chauki** postal system; tomb at Sasaram.
**Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** — Akbar (Bairam Khan) defeated **Hemu**.
**Jahangir** — married **Nur Jahan**; received **Captain Hawkins & Sir Thomas Roe** (English envoys).
**Shah Jahan** built the **Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid**; the architectural golden age.
**Aurangzeb** — greatest territorial extent; re-imposed **jizya (1679)**; died in the Deccan (1707).
mainsAngles: Trace the political consolidation and later decline of the Mughal Empire.

glossary.definition: Babur's memoirs written in Turki, a primary source for the early Mughal period.
The 1540-55 rule of Sher Shah Suri and successors, noted for administrative reforms adopted later by the Mughals.
Babur's flanking cavalry tactic combined with field artillery at Panipat.

blocks.text: The Mughals ran India's most **integrated pre-modern administration** — the **mansabdari service, Todar Mal's revenue settlement, and a provincial pyramid** — funding a **prosperous, monetised, trade-rich economy**; **Akbar's** liberal reforms are its high point.

rows: **Akbar's** ranking by **zat (status) & sawar (cavalry)**; transferable, salaried nobility; paid via **jagir**.
**Todar Mal's** system — measured land, classified soil, cash demand on a 10-year average (~1/3).
**Subah → Sarkar → Pargana → village**; Subedar, Diwan, Faujdar.
Abolished jizya (1564) & pilgrim tax; **Sulh-i-kul, Ibadat Khana, Din-i-Ilahi, Mansabdari, Rajput alliances**.

items: Mansabdari (zat & sawar) + Todar Mal's Zabti revenue = the two pillars to always cite.
Akbar's liberal policy (jizya abolished, Sulh-i-kul, Din-i-Ilahi) is the analytical core.

prelimsPointers: **Mansabdari** — Akbar's; ranks by **zat (personal) & sawar (cavalry)**; paid through **jagir**.
**Zabti/Dahsala revenue** — **Todar Mal**; cash demand on a **10-year average**.
Central ministries — **Diwan, Mir Bakhshi, Sadr-us-Sudur, Mir Saman**.
Provincial units — **Subah → Sarkar → Pargana → village**.
**Akbar** abolished **jizya (1564)**; **Sulh-i-kul** (universal tolerance); **Din-i-Ilahi (1582); Ibadat Khana** debates.
Economy — **monetised, silver-rich (dam & rupee), textile exports, karkhanas, flourishing towns**.
**Ain-i-Akbari / Akbarnama** by **Abul Fazl** documents the system.
mainsAngles: Analyse the mansabdari and revenue systems as the framework of Mughal administration.

glossary.definition: A Mughal service rank fixing status (zat) and cavalry obligation (sawar).
Todar Mal's revenue system setting a cash demand from measured land and a ten-year price average.
Akbar's doctrine of 'universal peace'/tolerance towards all faiths.

blocks.text: The Mughals raised **Indo-Islamic art to its zenith** — the **Taj Mahal and Fatehpur Sikri, the Mughal miniature school, Persian and translated literature** — a **Ganga-Jamuni synthesis** that peaked under Shah Jahan.

rows: **Fatehpur Sikri (Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal), Agra Fort, Humayun's Tomb** (predecessor of the Taj).
**Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Moti Masjid**; **pietra dura, charbagh, bulbous dome**; the marble golden age.
**Mughal miniature** (Persian Safavid + Indian) — peak under **Jahangir**; artists Mansur, Bishandas.
**Persian** (court language); **Baburnama, Akbarnama/Ain (Abul Fazl), Jahangir's Tuzuk**; Sanskrit translations (Mahabharata → Razmnama).

items: Akbar = Fatehpur Sikri/Humayun's tomb (charbagh, red sandstone); Shah Jahan = Taj/marble/pietra dura.
Miniature painting peaked under Jahangir (Mansur — nature studies).

prelimsPointers: **Humayun's Tomb** — first garden-tomb (charbagh), forerunner of the Taj.
**Fatehpur Sikri** — Akbar; **Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas**.
**Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid, Moti Masjid** — Shah Jahan; **pietra dura & white marble**.
**Mughal miniature painting** peaked under **Jahangir**; painter **Ustad Mansur** (flora-fauna).
**Persian** was the court language; Akbar's translation bureau rendered the **Mahabharata as Razmnama**.
Chronicles — **Akbarnama & Ain-i-Akbari (Abul Fazl), Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Jahangir)**.
Style = **Indo-Islamic synthesis** (arch-dome-minaret + Indian craft, charbagh gardens).
mainsAngles: Assess Mughal architecture and painting as the peak of Indo-Islamic synthesis.

glossary.definition: Inlay of semi-precious stones in marble, a hallmark of Shah Jahan's architecture.
The four-quartered Persian garden layout used in Mughal tombs like Humayun's and the Taj.
The Persian-Indian court painting school that peaked under Jahangir.

blocks.text: The **Bhakti Movement** was a **devotional reform current (7th–17th c.)** stressing **loving devotion to a personal god, equality, and vernacular worship** over ritual and caste. Beginning with the Tamil **Alvars and Nayanars**, it spread across India through **saguna and nirguna** saints, democratising religion and enriching vernacular literature.

rows: Tamil; **Vishnu (Alvars) & Shiva (Nayanars)** devotion — the earliest Bhakti (7th-10th c.).
**Namdev, Tukaram, Ramdas (Maharashtra); Shankaradeva (Assam)**; in Andhra — **Annamayya, Ramadasu, Vemana, Potana**.

items: Distinguish Saguna (Tulsidas, Surdas, Mira, Chaitanya) vs Nirguna (Kabir, Nanak, Ramananda).
Alvars/Nayanars = earliest (Tamil); impact = vernacular growth, social equality, Hindu-Muslim synthesis.

prelimsPointers: Earliest Bhakti — Tamil **Alvars (Vishnu)** & **Nayanars (Shiva)** (7th-10th c.).
**Nirguna** (formless god) — **Kabir, Guru Nanak, Ramananda, Dadu**.
**Saguna** (god with form) — **Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas), Surdas, Mirabai, Chaitanya**.
**Ramanuja** — Vishishtadvaita; **Madhva** — Dvaita; **Shankara** — Advaita.
Maharashtra saints — **Jnaneshwar, Namdev, Tukaram, Ramdas** (Varkari tradition).
Andhra Bhakti — **Annamayya (Tirupati), Bhadrachala Ramadasu, Potana, Vemana**.
Impact — **social equality, anti-ritual/anti-caste, vernacular literature, Hindu-Muslim synthesis**.
mainsAngles: Examine the social impact of the Bhakti movement in medieval India.

glossary.definition: Devotion to a personal god with attributes and form (e.g. Rama, Krishna).
Devotion to a formless, attribute-less god, as taught by Kabir and Nanak.
The earliest Tamil Bhakti saints devoted to Vishnu and Shiva respectively.

blocks.text: **Sufism** — Islamic **mysticism** seeking union with God through **love, devotion and self-purification** — spread across India via **silsilas (orders)**, above all the **Chishti and Suhrawardi**. Its **khanqahs, tolerance and vernacular devotion (qawwali)** paralleled the Bhakti movement and fostered **Hindu-Muslim synthesis**.

rows: **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer)** — founder in India; **Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi), Baba Farid, Salim Chishti**; simple, tolerant, sama (music).
**Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan)** — accepted state patronage & wealth (unlike Chishtis).
**Wahdat-ul-Wujud (unity of being — Ibn Arabi)**, love (ishq), pir-murid (master-disciple), khanqah.
**Qawwali (Amir Khusrau), Urdu, Hindu-Muslim harmony, vernacular poetry**.

items: Chishti (Ajmer, tolerant, no state patronage) vs Suhrawardi (Multan, accepted wealth/state) is the key contrast.
Wahdat-ul-Wujud, khanqah, sama (qawwali) and Hindu-Muslim synthesis = the influence.

prelimsPointers: **Chishti order** — introduced by **Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (dargah at Ajmer)**; avoided state patronage.
**Nizamuddin Auliya** (Delhi) — greatest Chishti; disciple **Amir Khusrau**.
**Suhrawardi order** — **Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan)**; accepted royal patronage & wealth.
**Wahdat-ul-Wujud** ('unity of being') — Sufi doctrine (Ibn Arabi).
Sufi institutions — **khanqah (hospice), silsila (order), pir-murid, sama (devotional music)**.
**Naqshbandi** order — **Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi** led an orthodox reaction against syncretism.
Influence — **qawwali, Urdu, vernacular devotional poetry, Hindu-Muslim synthesis**.
mainsAngles: Compare the Bhakti and Sufi movements and their role in cultural synthesis.

glossary.definition: A Sufi order or spiritual lineage linking master (pir) and disciples (murid).
A Sufi hospice/lodge that served as a centre of devotion, teaching and charity.
The Sufi doctrine of the 'unity of being' — that all existence is one with God.
